text: So to zoom out first, let's talk about what the problem is.

text: The problem is that agents are non-deterministic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With traditional software, you can read the code and you can tell with some degree of reliability what exactly that code is going to do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With agents, you have no idea.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents are non-deterministic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents take multiple turns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They make decisions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And even if you give them the exact same input, they're not going to give you the exact same output.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And even if they give you the exact same output, they might not have taken the same path to get there every single time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that means that your code isn't the source of truth for what does my agent do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Instead, the traces are your source of truth and your traces at scale are the source of truth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to have a whole bunch of data to tell you, on average, what is it that my agent does, not just this one run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because you are essentially flying blind when you are building agents.

text: This is what you get when you download the repo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You get a pile of code and a pile of commit messages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that used to be enough to tell you what was going to happen, but it no longer is.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What you get instead is traces.

text: Traces are, for those who missed the 101 session, traces very briefly are like log lines for AI applications.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every single thing that your application, your AI application does
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every LLM call, every tool call, every agent turn, all of those things become a trace.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Traces can be nested so that they hold other traces and those are what Arise works with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They are sent to our servers and we give you an easy visualization of what you're looking at.

text: You get the inputs, you get the outputs, you get a whole bunch of metadata, like how much does it cost, how long did it take, the things that you need to debug an agent in practice.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tracing gives you visibility for every step the agent took, and that is a huge leap forward just by itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you can see what your agent is doing, suddenly you can see that your agent is taking 10 turns to do something that you thought was really simple, or it's doing one turn that it doesn't need to do, or it's doing something very expensive, or it's taking 20 minutes to do something that you think it should take a minute to do.

text: That is the basic value of observability.

text: That is why observability is so popular before you get into any of the extra stuff that we're talking about.

text: The problem with traces is that humans are a bottleneck within the tracing loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you put an application into production, you get a trace.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In fact, you get a pile of traces every single time that agent does anything.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you put that into production and you have thousands of requests per second, that means that you have millions and millions of traces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can spot check those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can read your traces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can absolutely look at what individual things are doing in development.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In production, you become a bottleneck.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can't possibly get an overall sense of what all of your traces are doing by reading them one at a time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the solution, the traditional solution, and by traditional I mean 2025 solution to this, was evals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Evals are either code or, even better, another LLM that looks at what your agent is doing, looks at the entire trace, and says whether or not that was good or bad by some definition of good or bad that you define.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The thing about evals is that they come from LLMs, which means that the LLMs provide not just a score, a one or a zero, but also an explanation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They were like, you defined good, this was bad for this reason, and that is the basis of an entire improvement loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Evals can give you machine-readable
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or rather human readable explanations, which machines can read these days, which say this is why your eval failed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is what you could have done better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can feed that back into a coding agent, which can then make your software better automatically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can close the software development loop without you having to do anything once you've really cleverly defined what good looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can create this hill and your agent can climb it all by itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that brings us to the 2025 eval loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You go from no visibility to having traces, to having traces in evals, to being able to do manual improvements as a result of looking at your traces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the problem is in 2026 that humans become a bottleneck in the loop again because your evals are now dealing with enormous levels of scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your agents are pumping out code incredibly fast.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your applications are running at scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You've got more evals than you can possibly deal with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So even though evals were allowed you to compress thousands of traces down to eval scores, you've now got so many evals running that you can't stay on top of those as a human by yourself.
